title: The Boy Who Wanted to Meet Akbar
summary: A poor village boy uses clever answers to bypass palace guards and win an audience with the Great Mughal Emperor.
keywords: the boy who wanted to meet akbar
full_text:
In a small hamlet outside Fatehpur Sikri lived an observant twelve-year-old boy named Mohan, whose greatest ambition was to behold Emperor Akbar with his own eyes. However, ordinary village folk were strictly barred from the imperial red sandstone gates unless summoned for court disputes.

One morning, hearing that Emperor Akbar was inspecting the royal stables near the city walls, Mohan carried a clay bowl filled with fresh wild berries picked from the thorny hills. Approaching the royal perimeter, a fierce guard leveled a spear at his chest: 'Halt, peasant boy! What business do you have near the Shadow of God?'

Mohan bowed politely and said: 'Noble soldier, I bring a gift for the Emperor that no jeweler in Agra can provide.'

Akbar, overhearing the bold declaration from his horse, called the boy over: 'What is this gift, child, that my jewelers cannot match?'

Mohan presented his bowl: 'Sire, wild mountain berries, sweet as nectar, ripened by the sun and washed by morning dew. Your jewelers have diamonds, but they cannot create life or sweetness.'

Pleased by the child's poetic spirit, Akbar tasted a berry and smiled. 'You speak well, boy. But tell me—do you know how to tell a wise man from a fool?'

'Easily, Your Majesty,' Mohan replied without blinking. 'A wise man listens twice as much as he speaks, which is why nature gave us two ears and only one mouth. A fool speaks twice as much as he listens, believing the world hungers for his noise.'

Akbar laughed with joy. Birbal, who was standing beside the Emperor's stallion, nodded with deep admiration: 'Sire, this child possesses the seeds of true discernment.'

Akbar handed Mohan a golden coin and said: 'Go home, clever boy, and study your books with diligence. When you are grown, return to this court, for Hindustan is always in need of minds that see truth with clarity.' Mohan bowed low, clutching his treasure, having proven that intelligence knows no age or poverty.
